articles.title: I'm 12 and want to try protein powder - should I?
articles.summary: We asked experts how safe it is for children and teenagers to take protein supplements.
articles.body:
Twelve-year-old Ben is desperate to try protein powder but there's one hurdle: me, his mum.

"I've asked about 20 times and you just keep saying no!", he says, claiming it would make him "fitter and bigger" and that his male friends use it.

In recent years, there's been an explosion of products marketed as "high protein", including milk, yoghurt, breads, cereals, bars and powders.

Social media is flooded with adverts for various supplements, including protein powder.

As a health journalist, I'm sceptical and think at Ben's age he must be getting enough protein through his diet.

So, do experts think it's safe for pre-teens and teenagers or is a big, juicy steak just as good?

My sport-obsessed son, who already eats a healthy balanced diet, asks me about protein powder on a regular basis.

His friend Louis, 12, has been using protein powder once or twice a week for nearly a year, after a workout and on top of whole foods. His parents are aware of this.

"I think it's helped, it gives me more energy and it's helped me grow, probably," he says.

But Ben's other friend Otis, who is 13, is not keen on the idea and feels there is pressure on young people to take protein supplements.

"They might just start using them without thinking about the consequences or what effects it may have on them."

Proteins break down into amino acids that help the body grow and repair.

But your body can't make all the amino acids it needs on its own, so you need to get more - known as essential amino acids - through your diet.

For an adult with a healthy weight, the recommended daily amount of protein you should be eating is 0.75 grams per kg of body weight, according to the NHS.

A good rule of thumb is that the amount of protein you have for each meal should fit into the palm of your hand.

If you exercise a lot, and when you get older, you need more protein so you could have up to 2 grams per kg of body weight.

But do teens really need it if they're eating well?

For teenage boys and girls "you can get all the protein that you need from food alone", says registered dietitian Nichola Ludlam-Raine.

It is important that teenage girls, especially, get enough iron and calcium, so Ludlam-Raine says not to become overly focused on protein at the expense of other nutrients.

Protein shakes, powders or bars can be useful for some, including high-level athletes and those who have certain allergies, but they should not replace a healthy diet.

There can also be some unwanted side effects from using protein powders such as bloating, gas, cramps, and diarrhoea.

Those with pre-existing health conditions should not use it unless they have been told they can by their doctor.

Ludlam-Raine points out that the protein powder market is not as tightly regulated as medicines.

"Of course, you can get reputable companies who do third-party testing and make sure that what you see on the label is what is in the inside, but that's not always the case," she says.

"And ultimately you can't just have a shake and your biceps grow."

Some protein powders contain high amounts of added sugar, artificial ingredients, and hidden stimulants.

Dr Ramnik Mathur is a consultant paediatrician from Chelsea and Westminster NHS Trust.

He explains that we need micronutrients like zinc, calcium and magnesium, which are found in whole foods.

So, if meals are replaced with protein shakes, those nutrients are lost.

Experts suggest spreading out protein across the day and aiming for 20-25g per meal. If you're keen to up your intake, try some of these recipes.

During puberty when children have growth spurts, they do need more protein because their body is growing rapidly, building new muscle and bone mass.

But Mathur says there are risks to eating too much protein.

"If you look at social media, they'll say you need to eat a lot of protein, but your body can handle only so much."

He explains that if you eat too much, it has to be excreted by the kidneys and liver which can become overloaded.

Mathur explains: "We had a child here at the hospital where I work - he was taking so much protein that his kidneys just stopped working and he actually passed away."

The key takeaway from Mathur: "If a 12-year-old child is eating a healthy balanced diet then they shouldn't need any more protein."

Ludlam-Raine's advice is to get teens to improve their diet first before taking any protein powder, especially regularly.

If they still want to use it, speak to a registered dietitian or nutritionist first.

Now off I go to tell my son the answer is still no - and the experts say the same.

articles.title: 'Owned and controlled by US govt': Musk refutes Ukraine's charge of crippling Starlink
articles.summary: Elon Musk on Wednesday denied Ukraine’s allegation that SpaceX had disrupted its military drone operations by restricting access to its Starlink satellite
articles.body: Elon Musk on Wednesday denied Ukraine’s allegation that SpaceX had disrupted its military drone operations by restricting access to its Starlink satellite internet service without warning, saying any limits were imposed by the US government and not the company.“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” Musk said.His response came after Ukrainian military officials reported disruptions to Starlink connections on military-grade terminals moving at high speeds, complicating efforts to use the satellite internet service to guide drones.“Our defence forces did not receive a warning about this limitation, and this led to the disruption of several missions,” presidential adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov wrote on Telegram.Ukraine’s 7th Rapid Reaction Corps, deployed in the country’s south-east, said connections had been dropping for 10 to 20 seconds when drones travelled at speeds of 110 to 120 kmph.“The drones kept moving, but these interruptions made them harder to control,” the corps said in a statement to news agency Reuters.A source in Ukraine’s defence ministry said the restrictions had significantly complicated logistics and some drone operations.The reported disruption also drew criticism from Poland, which pays for Ukraine’s Starlink subscriptions. Polish foreign minister Radoslaw Sikorski directly challenged Musk over the issue.“Hey, @elonmusk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again?” Sikorski asked Musk on X. “As your European customers, we are watching you.”Musk did not immediately respond, while SpaceX did not immediately reply to a request for comment outside US business hours. Musk has previously referred to Sikorski as a “small man”.The dispute comes amid worsening relations between Kyiv and Washington after US President Donald Trump lifted sanctions on Russian diesel last week and criticised Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.Seeking to curb fuel prices that have risen since the US launched its war against Iran, Trump has urged Ukraine to stop attacking Russian oil refineries and suggested that Zelenskyy should be replaced.The reported restrictions have added to Ukrainian concerns that Washington and its allies could scale back military support to pressure Kyiv into making concessions to Moscow. articles.title: Mexican court closes case against official over 2023 detention centre fire
articles.summary: Victims’ groups, however, have denounced the ruling as ‘selective’ justice that exonerates the former migration chief.
articles.body:
A Mexican judge has closed the case against Francisco Garduno, former head of the country’s immigration agency, for crimes related to the 2023 fire at a Ciudad Juarez detention centre that killed 40 migrants and injured 30 others.

The incident was the deadliest event ever to occur at a Mexican immigration centre, and critics said it exposed the shortcomings and irregularities in the country’s detention system.

Garduno faced trial for the crimes of abuse of public office and dereliction of duty after footage from the fire showed guards had failed to respond to cries for help.

On Tuesday, Judge Victor Manlio Hernandez Calderon ruled that Garduno had fulfilled the court-mandated measures required to address the damage. But victims rejected that decision and announced they would appeal.

“Yesterday, corruption and the impunity of politicians protected by power won again,” the Foundation for Justice, one of the NGOs representing some of the victims, wrote on social media on Wednesday.

The victims have also compared the judge’s decision to close the criminal case to a de facto exoneration for Garduno.

In their view, the ruling “confirms that justice in Mexico is selective” and denies the victims “full reparations” and concrete guarantees that such an event will not be repeated.

Miguel Zenteno, one of the foundation’s lawyers, noted that the ruling is not yet final because it will be appealed and because another injunction is pending against the court-mandated reparations, which critics say failed to meet the standards for serious events.

On March 27, 2023, some 70 men were crammed into a locked dormitory with no ventilation and barely any water at the Ciudad Juarez immigration detention centre, on the border with El Paso, Texas.

As night fell, a small group set fire to some mattresses in protest, and within seconds, smoke engulfed the entire area.

Security cameras recorded the guards leaving the area despite cries for help. They made no attempt to open the gates of the dormitory. Only the women, held in another cell, were released. Most of the victims were Central Americans and Venezuelans.

Garduno, a former prison guard and current official at the Ministry of Education, led the National Migration Institute (INM) starting in 2019 and continued in the role until 2025 despite the fire.

The judge had previously ordered Garduno to compensate the families, provide them with free specialised medical care, issue a public apology, provide human rights training to migration personnel and guarantee that the events would not be repeated.

Zenteno acknowledged that the measures were implemented only partially because Garduno did not pay the damages as stipulated by the legal process.

Instead, Zenteno pointed out that the funds came from the INM, and the payments did not fully compensate the families. Furthermore, he added, the victims were not even informed how to access free medical services, and the apology “was a mere formality, not substantive”.

In addition to Garduno, prosecutors accused another former director of the institute of the same crimes.

Six immigration agents – including a military officer and a private security guard – and the two migrants accused of starting the fire are charged with homicide and assault. Most of the officials remain free pending trial.

articles.title: Costa Rica opens mega-prison as Bukele model embraced across Latin America
articles.summary: President Laura Fernandez says mega-prison is part of ‘tough-on-crime model’ embraced by her government.
articles.body:
Costa Rica has announced the opening of a new mega-prison amid near-record homicide levels and growing organised crime, as countries across the region embrace police crackdowns that have proven popular but often weaken key civil liberties .

President Laura Fernandez opened the High-Containment Centre Against Organised Crime, or CACCO, on Wednesday. The prison will have capacity for 5,100 people, equivalent to about 20 percent of the country’s current prison population.

“The CACCO will force criminals to face a new model – a tough-on-crime model. Costa Rica will become a global benchmark for prison security,” Fernandez said during an inauguration ceremony.

Candidates across Latin America have embraced mega-prisons, seeking to replicate the policies of Nayib Bukele , the president of El Salvador, who has won widespread popularity through a campaign of mass arrests and the suspension of basic rights in the name of combating crime.

Costa Rica , long spared from high levels of violent crime compared with its neighbours, saw a record-setting 905 homicides in 2023, followed by 876 in 2024 and 873 in 2025.

Analysts say that is partly due to increased fighting between criminal groups over lucrative drug routes.

The first transfers to Costa Rica’s new mega-prison will take place at the end of October, with Justice Minister Gabriel Aguilar saying the facility will help the government reassert control over the prison system and diminish infiltration by organised crime.

Right-wing leaders in other Latin American countries have also sought to replicate the mega-prison model.

Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori, inaugurated in July, has announced plans to tour El Salvador’s Terrorism Confinement Centre (CECOT), in anticipation of creating a similar facility in her country. CECOT can hold about 40,000 people.

In Colombia, meanwhile, newly elected leader Abelardo de la Espriella campaigned for the presidency, in part, on a pledge to build 10 mega-prisons. He took office in August.

Brazil, the largest country in Latin America, is currently in the midst of its own presidential election, and right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro has advanced to the final round of the vote. His platform also includes building five mega-prisons, citing the Salvadoran model.

El Salvador first imposed a “state of exception” under Bukele in 2022, expanding police and military powers.

That emergency declaration has been credited with a sharp drop in that country’s homicides, but rights groups say it has led to severe rights abuses and has been weaponised against critics of the government.

The “state of exception” has also resulted in mass arrests and mass trials, with rulings delivered against hundreds of defendants at a time. Some defendants have been detained without charge.

While the Bukele administration frequently touts its success in dismantling the gangs, the government has continuously extended the state of exception since it was first imposed.

Critics have warned that conditions inside mega-prisons are often poor, with imprisoned people facing overcrowding, due process violations and alleged torture in facilities like CECOT.

images.caption: Costa Rican President Laura Fernandez speaks during the inauguration of the High-Containment Centre Against Organised Crime (CACCO) in Alajuela, Costa Rica, on October 14, 2026 [Mayela Lopez/Reuters]

articles.title: Copper theft suspect's desperate escape caught on bodycam video before deputies discover what he left behind
articles.summary: Rayven Lee Wooten dove headfirst through a closed window to flee an Oklahoma deputy but left behind a backpack with a critical clue inside.
articles.body: An Oklahoma copper theft suspect stunned a deputy with a headfirst dive through a closed window, but overlooked one detail that helped deputies track him down. The encounter unfolded Oct. 1, when Oklahoma County Sheriff’s Office deputies responded to a burglary in progress at a vacant home on Sunset Lane, according to information included in the agency’s bodycam video. A deputy found Rayven Lee Wooten, 24, of Nicoma Park, inside allegedly stealing copper wire from a dishwasher, authorities said. "You’re not listening," the deputy said. "Turn around and get on your knees. You will get shot." Wooten instead ran around the kitchen and dove headfirst through the closed living room window, prompting a startled expletive from the deputy. "He just bailed out the window. He’s on foot," the deputy radioed. WATCH: WILD TRAFFIC STOP TURNS CHAOTIC AS SUSPECT DRIVES OFF WITH ONE COP INSIDE, DRAGS SECOND OFFICER Wooten initially escaped, but deputies said he left his backpack behind with his driver’s license inside, helping them track him down. The sheriff’s office had its own review of the dramatic getaway. "A suspect took the phrase ‘Make a break for it’ a little too literally!" the agency wrote alongside the video, adding that the man "missed his calling as a Hollywood stuntman." articles.body:
A watchdog group in a lawsuit on Wednesday challenged the legality of Jared Kushner’s role in his father-in-law’s administration.

“Primarily, this suit seeks to bar Kushner from occupying his government position and exercising government authority in violation of the Appointments Clause,” the lawsuit, from Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (CREW), reads.

“If not for this violation, Kushner would have been required to comply with transparency and conflict-of-interest obligations, including the filing of public financial disclosures during the appointment process,” the suit continues.

The Appointments Clause lets the president appoint “principal officers” that the Senate later confirms and allows courts or departments to appoint “inferior officers” with Congress’s permission. Kushner has not been confirmed by the Senate for his current government work.

In February, Trump said he was going to make Kushner a special envoy for peace . The president’s son-in-law returned to Trump’s second term to take part in specific talks, working toward a ceasefire between Israel and Hamas and crafting a Gaza peace plan for reconstruction and governance.

NewsNation, The Hill’s sister network, was later told by the White House that Kushner’s role was not official.

Kushner has worked with Steve Witkoff, a loyal Trump adviser whose role is special envoy for peace missions. Trump in February said Kushner would acquire the same title.

“We’re making Jared also envoy of peace. They’re both envoys of peace,” Trump said at the time.

The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment on the suit.

articles.title: Ship catches fire in Romania’s waters amid rising attacks in the Black Sea
articles.summary: Authorities are investigating whether drones may have been involved in the latest incident.
articles.body:
A ship anchored in Romania’s territorial waters has caught fire and the crew has been evacuated, Romanian authorities said.

The incident comes amid growing concerns over hybrid attacks in the Black Sea involving Russia.

Romanian Defence Minister Radu Miruta said on Wednesday it was unclear whether a drone had hit the ship, identified as the Comoros-flagged chemical and oil tanker Yara J, and that an investigation was pending.

Multiple drones breached Romanian airspace on Wednesday near its border with Ukraine.

On Tuesday, two ships were hit in drone attacks off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast, with one of them sinking, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said.

Radev said there was no clear evidence of who carried out the attack, but “the outcome benefits” Russia and that the Russian ambassador would be summoned over the incident.

Earlier this month, a grain ship caught fire and sank outside Romania’s territorial waters. Ukraine blamed Russian drones for the incident, in which two people were killed and 11 others rescued.

“A horrific strike by two Russian drones on a civilian vessel in neutral waters carrying corn and owned by Turkiye,” Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote on social media.

Some see incursions by Russian drones into eastern European airspace as a test of NATO and the European Union’s defences and response capabilities.

Romania, a NATO member, shares a land border with Ukraine. Since the Russia-Ukraine war started, drones have breached its airspace while mines floating in the Black Sea threaten key trade and energy routes.

Last Wednesday, Bulgaria’s President Iliana Iotova said she would invite Romania and Turkiye to consultations on ensuring the security of merchant ships in the Black Sea.

On October 6, two ships were hit in a drone attack in Bulgaria’s Black Sea exclusive economic zone. One sank and the other was damaged.

The crew of the damaged ship were rescued, but the crew of the sunken one remain missing. Bulgarian authorities ended search operations after confirming no survivors were found.

articles.summary: Police in Palatine, Illinois, arrested a 19-year-old man following an investigation into threats of a potential mass shooting at a Hindu temple.
articles.body: Police in Palatine, Illinois, arrested a 19-year-old man following an investigation into threats of a potential mass shooting at a Hindu temple.The investigation began on October 11, when the Palatine Police Department received information from the Mount Prospect Police Department about concerning electronic communications allegedly sent by Alexandros Paporakis.Investigators said Paporakis had shared a document outlining an alleged plan for a mass shooting at the Hindu temple. He also shared images of a rifle, magazines, body armour and other tactical gear and accessories.FBI investigators examined electronic communications and a document attributed to Paporakis titled “Why I Fought: A K A: (Aurora Shooter’s Manifesto).” The document contained white supremacist and extremist views, including references to violence against people of South Asian heritage, particularly those of Indian descent.Detectives believe Paporakis may have been planning an attack on October 11, possibly targeting a Hindu place of worship in the Aurora area. Police subsequently contacted Hindu places of worship within their jurisdiction to alert them to the threat.Paporakis was charged with one count of making a terrorist threat, a Class X felony, and one count of unlawful possession of weapons. He appeared for a detention hearing on Wednesday, where a judge ordered him to remain in custody."The seriousness of this alleged threat cannot be overstated. Through the immediate sharing of information and coordinated response by the Palatine and Mount Prospect Police Departments, officers were able to identify and take the suspect into custody. We are grateful for the FBI’s assistance in the subsequent investigation and commend the individual who initially came forward with this information. Protecting our communities and places of worship remains a priority, and we will continue working with our law enforcement partners as this investigation moves forward," Palatine Police Chief William Nord said, as cited by ANI.Paporakis was arrested as he was leaving his residence. During a subsequent search of his home, Palatine Police detectives recovered a rifle, multiple loaded magazines, hundreds of rounds of additional ammunition, tactical gear and other items believed to be relevant to the investigation.The recovered items included a tactical vest with body armour and a patch bearing imagery associated with white supremacist extremism.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: How Chinese parts are fuelling Houthi ambitions to strike Israel and Saudi Arabia
articles.summary: Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels are seeking to manufacture advanced ballistic missiles using components sourced from China, potentially giving the group
articles.body: Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels are seeking to manufacture advanced ballistic missiles using components sourced from China, potentially giving the group the ability to strike targets across Saudi Arabia and Israel, according to a new report by the Wall Street Journal.A separate investigation by Bloomberg has documented a wider supply network bringing missile parts, drone components and industrial machinery into Yemen.The findings point to the Houthis’ growing ambition to manufacture more of their own weapons instead of relying primarily on Iran for finished systems. However, the extent of their ability to produce advanced missiles independently remains uncertain.Chinese shipments reveal missile-building ambitionsThe WSJ report, based on findings from Conflict Armament Research (CAR), a group that traces weapons and their supply chains in conflict zones, said Yemeni authorities intercepted two shipments last year containing components needed to build a missile modelled on Iran’s Kheibar Shekan precision-guided ballistic missile.The cargo included custom-made metal parts for missile motors and airframes, stabilising fins and solid-propellant rocket motor components. Investigators also identified material used to make heat shields that protect missiles during atmospheric flight. Some of the components were specifically designed for missile production, while others had potential civilian applications.The Kheibar Shekan, first revealed by Iran in 2022, has a reported range of around 2,000km, potentially placing all of Saudi Arabia and Israel within reach. Its manoeuvrability is also intended to make interception by air-defence systems more difficult.Fabian Hinz, a senior analyst at CAR, told WSJ that the arrival of Chinese components suggested the Houthis were either already manufacturing missiles or attempting to do so. He cautioned that their heavily concealed weapons facilities made it difficult to establish how far production had progressed.A wider supply networkA September 23 investigation by Bloomberg examined four shipping containers seized at Yemen’s southern port of Aden. The cargo had been shipped from China and was bound for Hodeidah, a Red Sea port controlled by the Houthis.Weapons experts found suspected missile parts, drone components, control systems, launch equipment, computer-controlled machine tools, engines and tunnelling equipment. The material included rear fins resembling components used in Iranian ballistic missiles and phenolic resin, which can be used to manufacture heat-resistant missile shields.Fawaz Al Bsesi, director general of Aden’s Land, Sea and Air Ports Department, told Bloomberg that the components appeared to have been distributed across four containers to make them harder to detect. In a note to his superiors, he wrote that he had come across what appeared to be a complete missile structure spread across three containers.The investigation also identified a broader commercial network connecting Chinese exporters with cargo bound for Houthi-controlled territory. Shipping records reviewed by Bloomberg showed dozens of containers moving under 41 bills of lading. In 25 cases, the Yemeni importer named in the shipping documents was changed while the cargo was in transit. Aden authorities said the changes were intended to conceal the Houthi-linked companies behind the shipments.Some of the seized equipment could have legitimate civilian uses. But weapons experts said the combination of components pointed to a supply chain capable of supporting domestic missile and drone production.From Iranian weapons to domestic productionThe Houthis have expanded their arsenal over years of conflict with support from Iran and Lebanon’s Hezbollah. Between 2015 and 2019, they relied heavily on importing Iranian missiles in disassembled form and reassembling them. From 2020 to 2023, they increasingly imported components to assemble or upgrade weapons, including systems operated under names such as Burkan and Quds.Analysts say the group is now diversifying its procurement networks and developing greater domestic manufacturing capacity. Mohammed Albasha, founder of the US-based security advisory firm Basha Report, told The Wall Street Journal that the Houthis had expanded their supply chains, accumulated operational experience and incorporated artificial intelligence into software for their missiles and drones.Henry Thompson, a former expert on the UN panel monitoring sanctions on Yemen, said there was evidence that the Houthis had been importing components for solid-fuel ballistic missiles from China for at least two years. Medium-range ballistic missiles, he warned, could allow the group to strike deeper into Saudi Arabia with larger payloads than cruise missiles and drones.China has said it complies with the UN arms embargo on the Houthis and maintains controls on military exports and dual-use goods. The reports, however, raise questions about how specialised components and industrial equipment are reaching the group through commercial supply chains.The investigations suggest that the Houthis are seeking the components, machinery and procurement networks needed to build a more self-sufficient weapons programme inside Yemen.You use AI every day. articles.title: Tunisia: What has Kais Saied achieved economically in seven years?
articles.summary: Rising prices, unemployment and public debt test Saied’s economic promises.
articles.body:
For Tunisian taxi driver Houssam Oueslati, inflation has a price tag: The cost of keeping his car on the road.

In 2018, he paid about 35 Tunisian dinars ($13) for engine oil. Today, the same purchase can cost close to 100 dinars ($34). To maintain his income, he has had to work longer hours, spending more of his day behind the wheel to cover rising operating costs.

His experience points to a broader question facing Tunisia nearly seven years into Kais Saied’s presidency: What has changed in the economy, and how much of that change has improved people’s lives?

Saied came to power amid widespread frustration with the political establishment, promising a fairer and more accountable state. Since then, Tunisia has faced the economic consequences of the COVID-19 pandemic, volatile global food and energy prices, and geopolitical turmoil.

These shocks have complicated the country’s recovery, but they do not settle the question of how effectively the government has responded. The economy continues to grow, and overall unemployment has eased from its pandemic-era peak. Yet food prices remain a burden, unemployment among young people is high, and public finances leave the government with limited room to manoeuvre.

For Tunisians such as Oueslati, what matters most is not the headline growth figure but whether their earnings cover the cost of living.

The price of the engine oil Oueslati buys has increased by approximately 186%, according to figures he provided to Al Jazeera. For a taxi driver, this is not an isolated expense but part of the cost of staying in business.

The pressure extends well beyond transport.

Tunisia’s annual inflation rate reached 5.6% in September 2026, up from 5.4% in August and 4.8% in January, according to the National Institute of Statistics.

Food and beverage prices rose by 8.4% year on year. Poultry prices increased by 16.5%, fruit by 16.3% and lamb by 14.6%. Core inflation, which excludes food and energy, stood at 4.9%.

These figures help explain why inflation can remain painful even when its headline rate appears moderate. Inflation measures how quickly prices rise, not whether they are affordable. When prices rise faster than incomes, purchasing power falls. And even when inflation slows, households do not automatically recover what they have lost: Prices generally remain high unless they fall.

Economist Ridha Chkoundali argues that the cumulative effect of price increases is central to understanding the pressure on Tunisian families.

According to his estimates, average annual inflation was 6.8% between 2015 and 2021, compared with 8.1% between 2021 and 2026, indicating stronger inflationary pressures in the latter period.

The government has taken steps to ease the financial pressure. The Central Bank cut its key interest rate twice in 2025, bringing it down to 7%. But lower borrowing costs cannot, alone, restore purchasing power eroded by higher prices.

Chkoundali also argues that tighter access to credit has left consumers with fewer ways to manage expenses. Loans, banking facilities and cheques once allowed some households to spread payments over time, he says. Changes in financing conditions and cheque regulations have narrowed those options.

For families with little savings, essentials now consume more of the household budget, while access to short-term financial support may be more limited.

The challenge is not simply to bring inflation down, but to make everyday life more affordable and give households a chance to rebuild their financial security.

Tunisia’s economy grew by 2.3% year on year in the second quarter of 2026, according to the National Institute of Statistics. Growth reached 1.4% compared with the previous quarter.

The 2026 Finance Law had projected annual growth of about 3.3%, setting a more ambitious benchmark for the year.

For Chkoundali, the gap between the budget projection and the quarterly figures highlights a deeper problem: Growth matters to households only when it translates into greater production, investment, employment and income.

The labour market illustrates the challenge.

Tunisia’s overall unemployment rate stood at 14.9% in the second quarter of 2026, down from 15.3% in the same period a year earlier. It had reached 17% in 2020, according to the National Institute of Statistics.

But the headline rate conceals a harsher reality for younger Tunisians. Unemployment among people aged 15 to 24 reached 35.4%, while the rate among university graduates stood at 26.6%.

For many young people, the obstacle is not simply finding work. It is finding a job that offers reliable income, stability and a path towards independence.

If economic expansion fails to create enough productive jobs, its benefits will remain limited for large sections of the population.

Chkoundali identifies weak investment and declining production as major constraints. He also warns that the government’s reliance on domestic borrowing could make it harder for private businesses to obtain financing, expand and hire.

According to figures he cited, domestic borrowing amounted to about 7 billion dinars ($2.3bn) in both 2024 and 2025, with 11 billion dinars ($3.7bn) in borrowing at the beginning of 2026.

The concern is that the state’s financing needs could compete with private businesses for available credit. Domestic borrowing does not automatically undermine growth; its effects depend on the terms of financing and how the money is spent. But if businesses struggle to secure funds for investment, the consequences can be felt in production and employment.

Tunisia faces a difficult balancing act: financing the state’s obligations while creating conditions for private enterprise to grow and provide jobs.

For workers such as Oueslati, the consequences are immediate. When operating costs rise but earnings do not keep pace, longer hours can become a way of standing still rather than moving ahead.

Saied has made combating monopolies and speculation a central part of his economic agenda, presenting the campaign as a way to protect consumers, curb abusive practices and advance social justice.

The objective speaks to public frustration over rising prices. But critics argue that the authorities have not always adequately distinguished between speculative stockpiling and the storage necessary to keep essential goods available.

Warehousing, inventory management and distribution are integral to functioning supply chains. Restrictions that disrupt these systems without providing alternatives can, critics warn, contribute to shortages rather than bring prices down.

The risk is particularly significant in markets that depend on imports and distribution networks operated by private companies and public-sector entities. When stocks run low or supply channels are disrupted, goods can become harder to find even when government intervention is intended to protect consumers.

Enforcement may be necessary to tackle abusive practices, but it cannot replace the infrastructure and commercial systems needed to keep goods moving.

Protecting consumers therefore requires more than confronting speculation. It also requires policies that preserve reliable supplies, support production and ensure essential goods reach the market.

In a statement, the Democratic Current party criticised what it described as a refusal to confront economic realities, arguing that attributing failures to conspiracies would deepen the country’s problems rather than resolve them.

The government’s interventions must ultimately be judged by their results. A policy designed to protect consumers must be assessed not only by its stated purpose, but also by its effects on prices and availability of goods.

The government faces another constraint in its efforts to support economic activity and shield households from rising costs: The burden of financing the state.

Tunisia’s public debt rose from 67.8% of gross domestic product in 2019 to 84.9% in 2024, before falling to 82.1% in 2025, according to Finance Ministry data. The 2026 Finance Law projects a ratio of approximately 83.4%.

Debt levels alone do not determine whether public finances are sustainable. Borrowing costs, repayment schedules, government revenue and economic growth also matter. But substantial financing needs can leave the state with less flexibility to respond to new shocks.

Debt servicing competes with public-sector wages, social spending, subsidies and investment. The government must meet existing obligations while funding services and projects that could strengthen the economy over the longer term.

Chkoundali argues that the state’s financing needs have narrowed its options. The question is not simply how much the government borrows, but whether its financing choices leave enough resources for productive investment.

That pressure becomes more acute when international energy prices rise.

The cost of shielding consumers from oil prices

Tunisia’s 2026 Finance Law assumed a Brent crude price of about $63.30 per barrel. By the end of June, the average price had reached approximately $92.60, according to figures cited in the report.

The increase raised the potential cost of energy imports and fuel subsidies, putting additional pressure on public finances.

Fuel subsidies amounted to 2.427 billion dinars in the first half of 2026, equivalent to $826m. That represented 48.6% of the allocation for fuel subsidies under the Finance Law.

Public investment expenditure over the same period totalled 1.665 billion dinars, or approximately $566.6m.

The figures show how the government must balance competing demands on the budget. Subsidies shield consumers from some of the immediate effects of higher energy prices. But when oil costs more than expected, maintaining that protection becomes more expensive, potentially leaving fewer resources for public investment.

Cutting subsidies too abruptly could transfer more of the burden to households and businesses. Maintaining them, meanwhile, can intensify fiscal pressure when international prices rise sharply.

The consequences may extend beyond government spending. A larger energy import bill increases demand for foreign currency and may put pressure on the dinar and foreign-exchange reserves, particularly if export earnings and domestic production fail to offset the additional costs.

Chkoundali also points to trade imbalances involving partners including Algeria and Egypt as part of the wider external challenge.

He argues that policymakers should prepare multiple scenarios when estimating financing needs and subsidy costs, rather than rely on a single oil-price forecast. Such planning could help the government anticipate market changes before they place unexpected strain on the budget.

For Tunisia, the challenge is to shield households from external shocks without undermining the investment needed to make the economy more productive and less vulnerable to them.

Saied’s supporters argue that his economic record cannot be assessed without considering the problems that preceded his presidency.

Houssam Ben Ahmed, a political activist who supports the president, says Saied inherited a country already in serious decline across several sectors. He describes the measures taken on July 25, 2021 as “an absolute necessity to save the state”, citing what he sees as the fragmentation and deterioration of political and economic life.

From this perspective, the disruption that followed was part of a confrontation with longstanding problems, rather than evidence that Saied’s policies alone were responsible for the country’s difficulties.

The argument points to an important distinction in assessing any government’s economic record. The pandemic, international market volatility and geopolitical tensions have affected Tunisia, while structural weaknesses and political disputes long predate Saied’s presidency.

But inherited problems and external shocks do not remove the need to examine the decisions made in office. They form part of the context against which the government’s choices and results must be judged.

Has the government improved conditions for investment? Has it strengthened domestic production, created jobs and protected living standards? And where improvements have occurred, have they been sufficient to meet public expectations?

Supporters emphasise the difficulties Saied inherited. Critics point to persistent pressure on household budgets and limited opportunities for young people. A meaningful assessment must look beyond both claims to the evidence: What has improved, what has deteriorated and how much can reasonably be attributed to government policy?

Nearly seven years into Saied’s presidency, Tunisia’s economic record remains mixed. The economy continues to grow, and overall unemployment has eased from its pandemic-era peak. Yet food prices remain high, joblessness among young people persists, and public finances face competing demands.

External shocks have made recovery harder. But enduring a crisis is not the same as emerging from it. An economy can weather successive shocks without delivering the improvements in income, employment and security that people expect.

A more convincing recovery would mean stronger productive investment, more stable jobs, higher domestic production and incomes that keep pace with the cost of living. It would also require the government to manage its financing needs without sacrificing the investment on which future growth depends.

For Oueslati, the debate comes down to the cost of keeping his taxi on the road. Every increase in operating expenses eats into his earnings. Every additional hour behind the wheel is time spent trying to make up the difference.

One driver’s experience cannot determine the success or failure of an entire economic programme. But it highlights what national statistics can obscure: Whether people can turn their work into a more secure standard of living.

For Oueslati, progress would mean being able to keep his taxi on the road without having to work ever longer hours simply to make ends meet.

articles.title: Trump administration seeks to strip Ilhan Omar of US citizenship: WSJ
articles.summary: Investigators have subpoenaed relatives and examined immigration records, the newspaper reports.
articles.body:
The administration of US President Donald Trump is investigating Democratic Congresswoman Ilhan Omar to revoke her citizenship and eventually deport her, The Wall Street Journal has reported, citing US officials and people familiar with the investigation.

The inquiry centres partly on how the Minnesota representative obtained citizenship after arriving in the US as a refugee from Somalia, the newspaper reported on Wednesday. Authorities are examining her family’s immigration records and have issued more than a dozen subpoenas, including to some of her relatives, seeking testimony before a grand jury in Minnesota.

Omar’s office rejected the investigation as baseless in remarks to the Journal.

The Journal’s report comes just days after US federal agents raided the congresswoman’s home in what her office described as an “unprecedented escalation” by the Trump administration against its political opponents.

The search came just weeks before the November 3 midterm elections, a crucial vote for Republicans vying to retain control of Congress. Omar is seeking a fifth term representing Minnesota’s 5th congressional district.

The Department of Homeland Security said the raid was part of “an ongoing federal investigation”.

Agents took Omar’s passport, mobile phone, personal computers and notebooks, according to people familiar with the search, the newspaper said.

Omar arrived in the US in 1995 after living in a refugee camp in Kenya and became a citizen in 2000. She has previously denied committing immigration fraud.

At issue in the citizenship inquiry is whether Omar or her late father altered her age in immigration paperwork to indicate that she was 17 rather than 18 when her father applied for citizenship, the Journal reported.

According to the newspaper, investigators are examining whether that allowed her to acquire citizenship through her father rather than having to undergo a separate application process.

Omar’s father died in 2020, complicating efforts to collect evidence on whether Omar lied about her own age – which, according to a former top immigration official in the Justice Department, the Trump administration would hinge its case on – or whether her father lied on her behalf.

The Journal also reported that Homeland Security Investigations officials examined a similar allegation during the administration of former President Joe Biden but did not pursue it because they lacked evidence of fraud.

The newspaper did not report that anyone had filed a lawsuit seeking to revoke Omar’s citizenship. Such a case would require court proceedings, as the investigation itself does not revoke her citizenship or authorise her deportation.

The newspaper reported that a nonpartisan congressional watchdog had earlier cleared Omar of wrongdoing over disclosures that overstated her assets.

Agents from Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), part of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), searched Omar’s home under what the department called a “judicially authorized search warrant”.

On Monday morning, agents blocked off the street around Omar’s home and removed boxes labelled “Seized Property Evidence”.

Omar, a prominent progressive Democrat, has faced years of attacks from Trump and his allies over her Somali background and immigration history.

Hours after the Monday raid, Trump told reporters he had “nothing to do” with the search, saying it was “really up to the DOJ [Justice Department]”.

articles.title: Teenager dies as heavy rain floods Istanbul
articles.summary: Roads collapse and hospitals take in water as floods swamp Turkiye’s largest city, shutting schools and halting traffic.
articles.body:
A teenage boy has died after torrential rain battered Istanbul, flooding hundreds of homes, causing roads to cave in and bringing traffic to a near standstill in Turkiye’s largest city.

Footage verified by Al Jazeera showed a surveillance camera capturing the moment the 14-year-old boy was electrocuted in the Balat area of Istanbul’s Fatih district, after stepping into a puddle during heavy rain.

The footage showed the boy walking through puddles at the entrance of a car park before suddenly collapsing to the ground.

The Istanbul governor’s office said the boy was taken to hospital unconscious, but he died despite rescue attempts, noting that an investigation into the incident had been opened.

Istanbul Governor Davut Gul urged residents to stay at home on Thursday unless travel was necessary. He called on people living in basement flats to spend the night on higher floors and to avoid creek beds, underpasses and other flood-prone areas.

The governor’s office suspended classes across the city for Thursday and banned motorcycles from the roads, the Associated Press reported. State employees with disabilities and mothers with young children were placed on leave.

The motorcycle ban took effect at 9pm on Wednesday and would stay in place until further notice.

Turkiye’s Interior Ministry warned of sudden flooding in several provinces on Wednesday and Thursday.

About 8,000 personnel, along with 2,000 vehicles and construction machines, were deployed across the city, home to about 16 million people, Turkish outlet Daily Sabah reported.

The rain began on Tuesday evening after warnings from Turkiye’s weather service.

Water filled roads and underpasses, leaving vehicles stranded in several districts, including Esenyurt and Sultangazi.

Water also poured into homes, shops and basements.

Emergency services received more than 2,500 reports of weather-related incidents, Daily Sabah reported.

Authorities recorded 1,277 floods and 15 landslides, and 47 people were stranded. More than 800 homes, 280 businesses and 76 vehicles were affected.

Sections of road collapsed in the Eyupsultan and Gaziosmanpasa districts, the Turkiye Today news website reported.

Local media reported that passersby rescued a woman after floodwaters swept her along in Istanbul’s Esenyurt district.

Several neighbourhoods were affected, with roads submerged, vehicles stranded and homes and businesses inundated. Floodwater also reached two hospitals and poured through the ceiling of the Haciosman metro station. In Sultangazi, a primary school’s retaining wall collapsed while students were inside their classrooms.

No injuries were reported among students.

The heaviest rain fell in the Omerli area of Beykoz, on Istanbul’s Asian side, where nearly 194mm (7.6 inches) was recorded, according to Daily Sabah. Acting Istanbul Mayor Nuri Aslan said parts of the city received nearly 100mm (3.9 inches) in 12 hours.

Traffic density reached about 90 percent during the evening rush hour, and flights were operating normally, the newspaper said.

articles.title: Trump wishes Pope Leo speedy recovery after lung cancer diagnosis, speaks highly of pontiff's brother
articles.summary: President Donald Trump revealed Pope Leo XIV's brother is a friend and avid MAGA supporter with memorabilia "all over" his house while wishing the pontiff well.
articles.body: President Donald Trump wished Pope Leo XIV a speedy recovery Wednesday following his lung cancer diagnosis, revealing that he is friends with the pontiff's brother, whom he described as an enthusiastic MAGA supporter. Speaking to reporters aboard Air Force One while traveling from Arizona to Montana, Trump expressed optimism about the 71-year-old pontiff's recovery following surgery to remove part of his right lung. "I want to see Pope Leo get well. I hear the prognosis for that type of a problem. It's a cancer. It's big stuff. Anytime you have cancer," the president said. "But the prognosis seems to be good, I've watched. And we just want to wish him our love and our best wishes." POPE LEO XIV BEGINS HISTORIC 4-DAY VISIT TO FRANCE Trump then discussed his friendship with the pope's brother and his wife, describing them as enthusiastic supporters of the president. "His brother is a friend of mine, who's a great — he's a fantastic guy — and his wife. You know, they're big Trump supporters. They have MAGA all over their house," he continued. "And I can say that his brother loves him a lot. Loves the pope a lot, and that's good, but I just want to wish him well. Get better fast." The president's remarks came one day after the Vatican announced that Leo had been diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, a form of lung cancer, following surgery at Agostino Gemelli University Hospital in Rome. According to the Holy See Press Office, doctors removed the lower lobe of the pontiff's right lung during a procedure that lasted approximately 90 minutes. Doctors reported no complications. TRUMP TAKES AIM AT POPE LEO XIV MEETING WITH 'USELESS' CHICAGO MAYOR BRANDON JOHNSON AT VATICAN The Vatican said the cancer diagnosis was confirmed through an examination of tissue collected during surgery, consistent with findings from tests conducted before the procedure. Leo had previously disclosed that doctors discovered a small lump in his lung at an early stage and recommended surgery. Following the operation, he awoke normally and returned to his hospital room after a brief observation period, according to the Vatican. articles.title: North Korea says it tested cruise missiles designed to be fired from submarines
articles.summary: It’s unclear whether North Korea is capable of building the systems necessary for underwater missile launches, which would be more difficult for its neighbors to detect.
articles.body: SEOUL, South Korea — North Korea says it has test-fired cruise missiles designed to be launched from submarines as it continues to expand its military capabilities during a prolonged freeze in diplomacy with Washington and Seoul. North Korean state media said Thursday that the military tested two types of such missiles in the country’s eastern waters on Wednesday. The report described the weapons as strategic, implying an intent to arm them with nuclear warheads, but did not specify whether they were launched from an actual submarine or an underwater test platform. North Korean state media said the tests were aimed at assessing the readiness of the country’s underwater combat systems, improving the navy’s ability to carry out strategic missions and demonstrating the reliability of its nuclear deterrent. The South Korean military did not immediately comment on the tests. The launches extended a recent run in weapons demonstrations, including tests of various hypersonic missile systems on Sept. 20 and Oct. 3 that the North said were aimed at advancing its arsenal of weapons designed to overwhelm missile defenses in South Korea and Japan. North Korea for years has been developing various ballistic and cruise missiles designed to be fired from underwater. It has also claimed progress in recent months in building a nuclear-powered submarine that it intends to arm with nuclear-capable weapons, as leader Kim Jong Un turns his focus to strengthening the navy after a decade of expanding the country’s ballistic missile program. North Korea’s potential acquisition of a submarine capable of operating stealthily for extended periods and launching missiles from underwater would be a worrying development for its neighbors as such launches would be difficult to detect in advance. But there have been questions about whether North Korea, a heavily sanctioned and impoverished country, has the resources and technology needed to build such systems. North Korea in recent weeks has also conducted live-fire drills and commissioned a new warship as Kim continues to flaunt his nuclear weapons program while rejecting U.S. and South Korean offers to resume long-stalled diplomacy. Kim in recent years has halted all diplomacy and cooperation with South Korea and described it as a permanent enemy amid a yearslong stalemate in larger nuclear negotiations with Washington. He has so far rebuffed U.S. President Donald Trump’s calls to revive their diplomacy, which broke down in 2019. His government has called for Washington to abandon its “hostile” policy toward Pyongyang and drop demands for North Korea’s denuclearization as a precondition for talks.

articles.title: Desperate to clear toxic haze, Indonesia to douse its skies with dry ice
articles.summary: Authorities in South East Asia have turned to weather modification as fires blanket the region in smog.
articles.body:
As toxic smog continues to billow from wildfires in Indonesia's forests and peatlands, authorities are looking at an experimental way to disperse the haze.

A trial on Thursday will see an aircraft scatter pellets of dry ice - solid carbon dioxide - in the air above South Sumatra province, one of the regions worst hit by the haze.

Indonesia is battling its most dire wildfire season in a decade, as an unusually strong El Niño has exacerbated drought conditions and made flames harder to put out.

Amid increasingly urgent efforts to clear the hazardous air, authorities in Indonesia and neighbouring Malaysia have turned to various weather modification methods.

These include cloud seeding, a technique that speeds up the natural process of water vapour condensing inside of clouds by dispersing compounds such as silver iodide to form ice crystals.

Authorities have been carrying out such operations for weeks.

But Thursday's dry ice trial is different.

Rather than interacting with clouds to trigger rain, the dry ice is meant to "break down" haze in the lower atmosphere "so that it can rise upward", said Dudung Abdurachman, the coordinating minister for political and security affairs.

"If this trial is successful, we will continue with other areas that are central to the haze, such as Central Kalimantan and its surroundings."

The trial will involve 1.5 tons of dry ice, according to authorities.

Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto has called for agencies to step up efforts to extinguish the wildfires and mitigate the impact of toxic smog billowing from the hotspots.

New cloud seeding operations are also set to take place in Central Kalimantan - another haze-stricken area - on Thursday and Friday.

Meanwhile, firefighters on the ground are continuing to tackle out-of-control blazes and authorities have deployed dozens of helicopters to extinguish the wildfires - though these operations have at times been disrupted by poor visibility in the haze.

Residents across Kalimantan and South Sumatra are bearing the brunt of the toxic smog, with air in many cities turning a dusty amber.

Pollutants have also drifted across borders to neighbouring Singapore and Malaysia, raising public health concern as air quality scores soar to unhealthy levels.

In parts of Malaysia with particularly hazy air - including its capital Kuala Lumpur and the city of Johor Bahru, near Singapore - local authorities have conducted their own cloud seeding operations.

Last month, Indonesia granted permission for Malaysian agencies to enter its airspace for cloud seeding operations along the countries' shared border.

More than one million wildfire hotspots have been recorded in Indonesia this year, burning almost 900,000 hectares of land, according to independent forest monitoring platform Nusantara Atlas.

Indonesian police have named more than 200 individuals and nine companies as suspects in connection with the fires.

articles.title: Marathwada’s reservoirs run dry as water stocks plunge to 42.7%, lowest in state
articles.summary: Marathwada dams hold only 42.7% usable water, lowest in Maharashtra, down from 86.95% last year; medium and small projects worst hit after weak monsoon.
articles.body: Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar: Marathwada’s water crisis is deepening fast. Reservoirs across the region now hold just 42.7% of their usable storage capacity, the lowest among Maharashtra’s six divisions and barely half of last year’s level of almost 87%, according to water resources department data.The sharp fall has raised fears about the availability of drinking water in the months ahead, especially as wells, borewells, and smaller water sources dry up across several districts.The situation is most critical in the hundreds of medium and small dams that form the backbone of the region’s water supply network. While Maharashtra’s average usable storage stands at 62.1%, Marathwada continues to lag far behind.Large reservoirs in the Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar division are 58.3% full, down from 97.3% a year ago. Medium projects hold just 21.1% of their capacity, compared to 76.2% last year. Small projects are in the worst shape, with storage plunging to a mere 15.4% from 66.7% a year earlier.The deficit is a direct fallout of a failed monsoon. Jalna collector Ashima Mittal said the rains were simply not enough to recharge the region’s water bodies.“Due to rainfall deficit, the water bodies did not recharge. In the current scenario, we are making efforts to raise public awareness about using water judiciously, while also keeping a check on illegal drawing and lifting of water from water bodies. Drinking water is and will remain our priority,” she said.With the water situation worsening, district administrations have already begun taking precautionary measures. Dharashiv collector Keerthi Kiran Pujar said authorities are moving to secure every available source of drinking water.“Already, wells and bore wells are being acquired to maintain steady drinking water to even the last person residing in the remotest corner of the district,” he said.The numbers underline the scale of the challenge. Large dams in the region currently hold about 2,630 million cubic metres of water against a capacity of more than 4,500 mcm. Medium projects hold just 223 mcm, while small projects contain only 269 mcm.In contrast, water-rich Konkan has reservoirs filled to 88.9% of capacity, followed by Pune at 82.9% and Nashik at 80.3%. Even Nagpur and Amravati divisions, which have also witnessed rainfall concerns, are significantly better placed than Marathwada.The widening gap has left Marathwada staring at difficult summer months before they have even begun. With drinking water now the top priority, authorities are racing to conserve every available drop.Stay updated with the latest Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar news. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: Two cargo ships sunk in Strait of Hormuz as Iran ramps up attacks in run-up to midterms
articles.summary: Two cargo ships have sunk near the Strait of Hormuz in the past 24 hours after being struck by unknown projectiles in separate incidents – highlighting the heightened danger to shipping as Iran steps up attacks in an attempt to regain control over the critical waterway.
articles.body: Two cargo ships have sunk near the Strait of Hormuz in the past 24 hours after being struck by unknown projectiles in separate incidents – highlighting the heightened danger to shipping as Iran steps up attacks in an attempt to regain control over the critical waterway. The Singapore-registered container ship GFS Pride was struck on Tuesday while passing through the strait, catching fire and later sinking, according to the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore. All crew members were safely evacuated. Videos verified by CNN show black smoke rising from the ship as it takes on water, while later footage and satellite images show cargo scattered in the water and a small oil slick. Iranian state media Press TV reported that the ship had “hit a sea mine on an unauthorized route” – which experts cast doubt on, saying a drone attack was more likely. The merchant vessel Cape Dao, registered under Antigua and Barbuda, also sank, according to data from the International Maritime Organization (IMO) on Wednesday – after it was first hit by projectile on September 23. One Indian crew member was killed. While many vessels have been hit in the Strait of Hormuz this year, these are only the second and third to have sunk in the Middle East since the Iran war began in February, according to IMO data. Attacks have ramped up significantly since the end of September, once again reducing the amount of oil transiting out of the Middle East and raising oil prices around the world. That’s been a consistent headache for US President Donald Trump as the midterm elections approach, with gas prices, tariffs, and other factors driving up the cost of living top of mind for many voters. Data from the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO), which monitors shipping incidents, shows just how high the risk is. Nine attacks in or near the Strait of Hormuz have been reported since Monday, including a drone strike on a tanker. Only 4.147 million barrels of oil successfully transited the Strait of Hormuz on Monday – less than a quarter of pre-war levels, according to maritime data tracking service Kpler. And the seven-day average of oil flow through Hormuz has dropped sharply since early October, Kpler’s data shows. “The sinking of Singapore-flagged GFS PRIDE marks a dangerous escalation after weeks of near-daily attacks on commercial shipping. Iran claims a naval mine; but a drone strike is more likely,” said former US Navy officer Charlie Brown, also a senior adviser for United Against Nuclear Iran, a nonprofit that tracks and reports on Iranian sanctions violations. “Many ask what response will the US Navy mount to Iran’s escalating attacks on global shipping,” he added. “But the real question is what response will other nations take? How long will the world tolerate this threat to shipping, seafarers and freedom of navigation?” The US military continues to enforce a blockade on Iranian ports to maintain economic pressure on Iran. To some extent, it’s worked: Iran’s economy is in tatters, and in recent months it clearly lost its leverage over the strait, with the amount of oil flowing from other Gulf nations through the waterway increasing to near-normal levels. That’s partly thanks to a complex operation involving US-military-escorted “dark” transits across the strait at night, with tankers turning off their transponders to avoid detection. That rise in oil flow is why Iran is now ramping up its attacks and threats, hoping to wrestle back the leverage it once had over the strait – especially as American voters head to the polls. The Trump administration has tried to lower prices in other ways, including a controversial deal announced last week to drop some sanctions on Russia to import a relatively small amount of the country’s diesel. But this has been met with bipartisan criticism – and there’s no guarantee it will bring any substantial relief, with analysts warning that diesel could climb near all-time highs by November.

articles.title: X suspends 13,000 accounts, alleging foreign influence ahead of US midterms
articles.summary: The social platform says networks targeted US political debate across the spectrum ahead of midterm elections.
articles.body:
The social media platform X has suspended more than 13,000 accounts related to three suspected foreign influence operations linked to Iran, Russia and China that sought to shape the political debate in the United States.

The company announced the suspensions on Wednesday as it outlined measures ahead of the November 3 US midterm elections.

X said its investigations found the networks used fake accounts to post and amplify political content targeting candidates and public figures “across the political spectrum”.

The company said it identified the accounts through “proactive sweeps and investigations” under its rules against spam and coordinated inauthentic behaviour.

“Free speech is the bedrock of a functioning democracy, and we are proud that X is the global town square where these debates happen. Our job is to keep that conversation authentic, open, and safe,” X Global Government Affairs said in announcing the suspensions.

X also outlined rules against misleading information regarding how, when or where to vote in the US midterms, as well as attempts to suppress turnout and voter intimidation, including calls for violence near polling stations.

The company said users can report election-related posts through the “civic integrity” option to request a community note providing context. In urgent cases, X may also apply labels to posts that violate its election rules in cases requiring attention, the platform said.

The announcement comes a week after OpenAI said it had shut down two alleged influence operations from Russia and Iran that used ChatGPT to push fake journalist personas and run a “think-tank” that covertly spread anti-Ukraine propaganda.

X has previously acted against suspected foreign influence networks. In 2021, Twitter, as X was then known, said it had suspended 238 accounts purportedly operating from Iran.

articles.title: Australian woman charged with lacing colleague's curry with snail poison
articles.summary: The alleged victim, who was in a relationship with the woman, had spotted bright green pellets in the meal.
articles.body:
An Australian woman has been charged after allegedly lacing a colleague's curry with snail poison.

Police in the state of Western Australia say the alleged victim made a meal for her co-workers in February, which they shared at morning tea.

But when the 58-year-old returned to eat leftovers at lunch, she noticed bright green granules in the food and that her tongue felt numb after tasting it.

The accused - who was in a relationship with the alleged victim - has been charged with endangering the life, health or safety of another person after a months-long investigation, and will face court on 5 November.

Police allege the 43-year-old woman - who hasn't been named - visited a chemical storage shed before returning to the staffroom where the curry was kept.

After tasting it, the alleged victim handed the meal over to detectives, who identified the substance as snail pellets containing metaldehyde, a poisonous substance.

Commissioner Col Blanch told reporters the poison can cause serious injury or death.

"We're just very thankful that the person who tasted the curry was aware of something that wasn't quite right," he said, according to the Seven Network.
